A controlled clinical trial conducted by the Cannabis-In-Cachexia-Study-Group in 2006 concluded that synthetic THC or low doses of cannabis extract administered orally for cancer-related cachexia (characterized by anorexia, weight loss, and emaciation) were not more effective than a placebo. 2. The accumulated data suggest that cannabinoid drugs may have therapeutic potential, particularly for symptoms such as pain relief, nausea and vomiting control, and appetite stimulation. 3. There is currently no convincing evidence to support the concern that medical marijuana use would lead to an increase in recreational use. Existing data suggest that this would not be an issue if medical marijuana use were regulated as strictly as other medications with abuse potential. 4. A survey of oncologists revealed that 44% had illegally recommended marijuana for controlling vomiting, 48% would do so if it were legal, and 54% believed it should be available by prescription. 5. THC has been shown to combat the formation of arterial blockages, as reported in a 2005 study published in Nature. 6. A study involving 56 patients who had not responded to other antiemetics found that 72% experienced success with smoked marijuana. The study also concluded that smoked marijuana was more effective than oral THC pills. 7. A double-blind controlled study published in 1979 found a 72% reduction in nausea and vomiting among cancer patients receiving high-dose methotrexate. The study also concluded that smoked marijuana was more effective than oral THC. 8. Three studies (Foltin et al., Greenberg et al., and others) demonstrated that marijuana use increases appetite and caloric intake in humans. 9. A 1975 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine concluded that smoked marijuana was more beneficial than synthetic THC for some cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. 10. Frequent marijuana use can cause airway injury, lung inflammation, and impaired pulmonary defense against infection. This is particularly concerning for patients with AIDS, as it may increase the risk of life-threatening pulmonary infections in immunocompromised individuals. 11. The immunosuppressive effects of THC raise the possibility that regular marijuana use could accelerate the progression of HIV infection, although this remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. 12. A 1979 study published in the Medical Journal of Australia found that delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) had anti-nausea and anti-vomiting effects in children receiving cancer chemotherapy. 13. A randomized comparison study published in 1980 in the New England Journal of Medicine found that THC was effective as an antiemetic in patients receiving chemotherapy for cancer, with results comparable to or better than prochlorperazine.
